_comment: Interview behavior playbook — the 8-step say-this-in-the-interview ritual. Read-only reference; SR over these items lands in Phase 4.

cards.title: Read the problem fully. Restate it back.
cards.body: "So, just to confirm — I'm given X, and I need to return Y, with constraints Z. Is that right?" This catches the 30% of cases where you misread the problem.

cards.title: Ask 2 questions BEFORE coding. Always.
cards.body: Input bounds? (10? 10⁴? 10⁹? — changes the algorithm) — Special inputs to handle? (Empty? Negative? Duplicates? null?) — Can I mutate the input?

cards.title: State brute force, then state optimal, BEFORE coding.
cards.body: Out loud. Even if obvious. "Brute force is O(N²) — nested loop. We can do better with a hash map — O(N) time, O(N) space. I'll code the hash map version." This is the #1 thing interviewers grade for "did they think before coding".

cards.title: Code, narrating in chunks.
cards.body: Don't dictate every character. Say: "Now I'll loop over the array, looking up `target - x`..." then code.

cards.title: Test against 3 inputs, on paper.
cards.body: The example given, an edge case (empty / single element / max), and one tricky case (duplicates / negatives / wrap-around).

cards.title: State complexity at the end. Time AND space.
cards.body: "This is O(N) time and O(N) space."

cards.title: Vocalize.
cards.body: "Let me think out loud about what's blocking me." Silent stuck = no signal. The interviewer can nudge you if you're vocal.

cards.title: Listen for the follow-up.
cards.body: Interviewer almost always asks: "Now do it in O(1) extra space" / "What if the input is streaming?" / "What changes if duplicates are allowed?" The follow-up is THE evaluation — not the first solution.
